items.title: What is included with Owner?
items.body: Both plans include all of our features. The Owner platform upgrades your online presence to drive direct orders like the top restaurant brands. You get an AI-powered website, world-class online ordering, and your own branded app. You also get proven marketing automations that drive reorders and repeat customers.

items.title: What commissions do I pay as a restaurant?
items.body: On our Flat plan, you pay a monthly subscription with no additional restaurant fees. On our Flex plan, you pay a lower subscription cost plus a 5% restaurant fee on orders. On both plans, guests pay a 5% order support fee that covers fulfillment and customer service. When your customers order from third-party apps, they're charged fees up to 15% of their order, so they'll pay less when they order directly from you.

items.title: Can I ever switch plans?
items.body: Yes, you can switch plans anytime. Some restaurants start on Flex and move to Flat as their online orders continue to grow with Owner.

items.title: Do you require any contracts?
items.body: No, there are no long-term contracts or commitments. You can use Owner month to month, and cancel at any time if you’re not seeing the results you want. At Owner, we don’t believe in locking restaurants into contracts. That’s why we have the only month-to-month billing in the industry—with no cancellation fees.

items.title: How long does it take to get started?
items.body: Many restaurants can launch within a week. We'll ask you for details like your website domain, Google Business Profile, and Yelp information. If you have those on hand, we can launch your new online presence with Owner in a few days.

items.title: Should I stop using third-party delivery apps?
items.body: Most of our customers use third-party apps alongside Owner. They use the apps as another marketing channel, then drive their customers to order directly from their Owner website and branded app.

items.title: How is Owner POS different from legacy POS systems?
items.body: Most POS systems focus on processing payments and back-office operations. Owner POS does that too, but it is built around a different idea: your POS should help grow your sales, not just ring them up. Owner POS captures guest info at checkout, drives app downloads, and puts every walk-in customer into automated marketing that brings them back.

items.title: How does Owner POS get in-store guests into my marketing?
items.body: At checkout, guests see their loyalty points climb as items are added to their order. To earn those points, they just enter their phone number. About 50% of customers do. From there, Owner sends a text to download your branded app and adds them to your marketing automatically.

items.title: Can I run in-store and online on one system with Owner POS?
items.body: Yes. In-store orders, online orders, and delivery all run through Owner. Your staff uses one screen. Your customers earn and redeem loyalty points no matter how they order. And because everything shares the same system, every channel feeds into the same marketing that brings customers back.

items.title: How long does setup take?
items.body: For most customers, just a few business days after receiving their hardware. Setup happens over one remote call. Your online menu imports automatically, so you do not have to rebuild it. No IT specialist required.

items.title: Do you require any contracts?
items.body: No, there are no long-term contracts or commitments. You can use Owner month to month, and cancel at any time if you’re not seeing the results you want. At Owner, we don’t believe in locking restaurants into contracts. That’s why we have the only month-to-month billing in the industry—with no cancellation fees.

items.title: How much does Owner POS cost?
items.body: We have flexible pricing that depends on the volume you’re doing today. Reach out to us for a quote customized to your restaurant!

Builders Wanted.
body: Mega corporations have thousands of engineers. The 33 million small businesses they're crushing have zero. We're the builders on the other side of that fight.

content.heading: We want you if:
body: You'd rather ship something a restaurant owner uses tomorrow than something a committee reviews next quarter.
You want problems that don't have a playbook, building AI that runs a business, not a feature that demos well.
You measure your work in customer outcomes: orders, revenue, a business that survives.
Big corporations are getting stronger with technology. Everyone else gets left behind.

The last era of tech produced powerful software. But software that demanded time, budget, and expertise to master. Enterprises could afford all three. Small businesses couldn't, and fell further behind every year. AI changes this. For the first time, we can build technology that doesn't require expertise, We build technology that simply delivers outcomes.

That's what Owner is: a complete system that delivers the one outcome small business owners need: profitable sales growth. Owner optimizes itself, using data from millions of interactions on our platform, so our customers never have to become technologists to compete with companies that employ thousands of them. We're building a future where everyone can win, not just the largest corporations.

content.heading: Without Owner, here's what that takes:

body: To get found, Yuliana needs to optimize her website for 100+ constantly changing factors in Google's local search algorithm, keep her info current across dozens of directories, and now show up when people ask ChatGPT where to eat. That's a full-time SEO team's job.

To drive repeat orders, Yuliana needs to know who her regulars are. But her online customers are invisible — hidden behind third-party apps or sitting on an email list she never has time to use. She needs to reach her best customers directly, and reward them for coming back, without it becoming another job.

Yuliana needs an ordering system that optimizes for lifetime value, not single transactions — a checkout that uses purchase history to suggest pairings, handles complex catering orders, and keeps improving as her customers' behavior changes.
Goliaths like Domino’s win because they have builders solving these exact problems.
Hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of them. Compare Domino's ordering experience to your favorite local pizzeria's. No contest.
Yuliana can't hire engineers, PMs, or marketers. She's one person running a restaurant while Goliaths optimize every advantage. That's where Owner comes in.
We're using AI to build for millions of Yulianas.

content.heading: Technology has been weaponized against local owners.
body: Local brick-and-mortar business owners are being destroyed by huge corporations. They're using tech and AI to crush and dominate small, independent businesses. Let's meet an owner from a local taqueria. His name is Mo, and his restaurant is Talkin' Tacos.
He started Talkin' Tacos in Florida in 2021. But he was off to a scary start against Goliath-sized corporations.
Taco Bell had huge tech and marketing teams to grow their business.
Mo had a mess of time-consuming tools. That's why he signed up for Owner.
20 years ago, the chile-roasted aroma would’ve been enough to bring in a steady stream of hungry customers. Mo’s great food and service could keep them coming back.

Around 2020, everything changed. The world shifted online. It was already shifting; Covid made it happen even faster. ~77% of restaurant ordering decisions are now made online. People find restaurants online. They buy online. It isn’t going to change back. The same thing is true for other types of local businesses, including salons and gyms.

But restaurants are living in the future. The shift hit them first and hardest because they’re the biggest category of brick-and-mortar businesses. Billions of dollars in capital have been deployed to shift consumer behavior toward high-tech experiences.
In this new world, food and service alone don’t stand a chance. Restaurant owners need to be digitally native experts to make it.

content.heading: Founding product insight
body: Owner’s key insight is that local business owners don’t need another software tool to figure out. They need an outcome: profitable sales growth.

All small business technology before Owner was built to be maximally customizable. But Owner optimizes for performance, not customizability. There’s a word now for the way Owner has been building software for the past 6 years: agentic. Owner’s product has a scientifically tested opinion on how to drive sales. It executes the best decisions on behalf of its customers.

For example, restaurant owners can change the logo and colors displayed by their Owner-powered website. But they can’t change the placement of CTA buttons, information hierarchy, or order conversion flow. They can’t change the things that impact performance.

The standardized system allows Owner to run thousands of split-tests. It’s impossible to run split-tests on surfaces you don’t control. But since Owner controls the websites and apps, Owner can rapidly iterate to improve them for everyone. Owner learns continuously while it works to deliver the outcome.

Owner tips the scales between life and death for Mo and others like him. They see 40%+ growth in their online order volume within their first year. They see a swift surge in sales, and also ongoing growth over time.
When Mo uses Owner, his customers prefer ordering from him. That’s because it satisfies cravings better, costs less, and feels just as easy as ordering from Taco Bell.

Mo's online sales grew so much that he asked Owner to run his in-store sales too. Now he uses Owner POS. Owner powers not only his online sales, but in-person sales too. Online success was the proof. That's what led Mo to make Owner his point of sale and system of record.

body: Ashley Lee runs Ashley's Cafe in San Francisco with plans to expand to seven locations. After partnering with Owner, she added $30K in monthly sales, tripled her walk-in capture rate, and grew branded app sales.

content.heading: How Their Online Experience Changed
content.subheading: Tablet chaos at every rush hour
body: Square, Uber Eats, DoorDash, the phone line, and in-person orders all ran on separate tablets. During peak hours, the noise and confusion led to mistakes and complaints from guests.

Ashley's old POS captured roughly one in five guests. Everyone else paid and walked out the door with no way to be reached again. She tried collecting emails on a paper notepad to fix it, but it never produced real repeat business.

items.title: One screen for every order
items.body: Delivery apps, the website, phone orders, and in-person checkout all flow into one screen. No more five tablets ringing at once during a rush. Tickets line up in order, kitchen-ready.

items.title: Loyalty rewards built into checkout
items.body: Guests join rewards by entering their phone number at checkout. Ashley now sees who's a first-timer and who's a regular, and she has a real audience to market to instead of names on a paper notepad.

items.title: Automated marketing that brings guests back
items.body: Right after checkout, customers get a text to download Ashley's branded app. From there, automated push notifications, texts, and emails keep them coming back. Monthly app sales grew about 44% after adding Owner POS.

content.heading: How Mattenga’s Pizzeria drove $192,000 in 30 days with Owner.com
body: Matt and Enga, engineers turned restaurateurs, founded Mattenga's Pizzeria in 2014. After partnering with Owner, they grew sales by almost $200k in one month, boosted Google visibility, and drove thousands of branded app downloads.

content.heading: How Their Online Experience Changed
body: Clicking “Order Online” sent guests offsite, so Google treated checkouts as offsite. This hurt Mattenga's Google rankings even even with ~1,500 reviews.
Before launch, they didn’t have a customer app—guests couldn’t enjoy saved payments, rewards reminders, or quick reorders.

items.title: Top-ranking website on Google
items.body: On-domain ordering keeps customers on their site. AI-generated landing pages for every neighborhood and menu item dramatically improved search rankings.

items.title: Branded mobile app
items.body: Mattenga's now lives on customers' phone home screens. Push notifications and loyalty rewards keep regulars coming back more frequently. After their app launched, Mattenga's drove $2,500 in additional sales on Day 1.

items.title: All-in-one automated platform
items.body: One system handles website, ordering, marketing, loyalty, and operations across all 7 locations. Automated campaigns run themselves, freeing up Enga's time for her top priorities and for family.

content.heading: SEO for Restaurants: The Complete Guide to Restaurant SEO (2026)
body: Our best SEO tips for busy restaurant owners who want to get more traffic from Google.

When it comes to getting more customers, most restaurant owners focus on social media, ads, or flyers, but the most powerful tool is often overlooked: restaurant SEO. Ranking high in Google searches puts your restaurant in front of people who are already hungry and ready to order.
SEO doesn’t have to be complicated. Most guides are written for marketers, not busy restaurant owners, but with the right approach, even a small team can see real results.
In this post, I’ll cover everything you need to know about SEO for restaurants, reveal 4 big wins that can drive more orders, and show exactly how to put them into action.

Here are answers to some of the most common questions we hear from restaurant owners about SEO. These tips focus on local search, keywords, and website structure to help your restaurant get more visibility and orders.

Make sure your name, address, and phone number are accurate and consistent across Google and all other online directories. Add high-quality photos, keep your hours up to date, respond to reviews, and use relevant keywords in your business description. These steps help Google understand your restaurant and show it to local diners.

Focus on keywords that combine your cuisine, signature dishes, and location, like “best pasta in [City]” or “authentic Italian restaurant in [Neighborhood].” Include these in your homepage title, main headline, and menu pages to capture local search traffic.

Use text-based menus rather than PDFs or images so Google can read your content. Organize items by category (e.g., appetizers, entrees, desserts) and naturally incorporate your keywords into dish names and descriptions. Make sure each menu page is easy to navigate on mobile and includes clear calls to action, such as “Order Online” or “Reserve a Table.”

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.
Take back control of your margins, customer data, and online reputation.

content.heading: How to Build a Restaurant Website (Step by Step)
body: Discover easy ways to build a website that attracts more customers to your restaurant.

You know what's tough for many restaurant owners? Building a restaurant website from the ground up. You’ve got a restaurant to run and aren’t a web developer, so why waste time trying to build a site that may not even work?

Don’t worry, there are website builders specifically for restaurants that make it fast, easy, and affordable to build a restaurant website that will actually get results and increase your sales. Instead of shelling out hundreds or thousands of dollars to a web developer, these tools can help showcase your menu, take online orders, and include promotions for a fraction of the time and cost.
I’m a firm believer that a good website will have the highest return on investment for your business, so I created this guide to teach you step-by-step how to build a restaurant website.

A restaurant website builder is like a cheat code for skipping all the hassle and intimidation of starting a website from scratch. Instead of dealing with time and attention-draining tasks like picking a domain name, figuring out web hosting, and picking a content management system, restaurant website builders offer tools that will seriously lighten your load and free up more time for what really matters: your restaurant and your customers.

Your restaurant website should be easy to update, and, most importantly, should get more customers into your restaurant. I'm here to help walk you through options that we've recommended to restaurant owners before. Plus, you can check out our roundup of the best restaurant websites to help steer you in the right direction.

Owner.com is a great choice for restaurants that want to make a website that drive more direct online orders. The platform provides more than just a basic online presence. It rebuilds your entire restaurant website with search engine optimization in mind so that customers can find you, resulting in more orders and boosted sales.

It also features an online ordering system designed to convert and make upselling easier. Owner.com can be a great fit for you if you’re already getting sales through third parties and want to turn your efforts into getting direct orders through your website.

My team and I did thorough research and testing to ensure that Owner.com is simple to use and attracts more customers. Our platform features a simple design template made specifically for driving sales — it’s so easy to use that even those with limited technical skills can navigate it. However, if you’re looking for a larger selection of template options that you can customize, I’d recommend looking elsewhere.
Owner websites come with an online ordering system that drives direct sales.

Once you’ve chosen your website builder, you’re ready to begin adding elements that will make your site more visible to customers. This can be done through search engine optimization (SEO) — I’ll show you what this is, how you can do it and why it works below.
SEO is your friend when it comes to your restaurant website and can help customers find you. SEO is the way that you tell search engines (Google, Bing, Yahoo, etc.) what your website is about.
To help your website stand out more and attract more visitors, we made this SEO for restaurants guide with steps for a more useful and effective website, including:
Notice how Upper Crust uses relevant keywords on their homepage.
To make things easier, Owner.com’s restaurant website builder has SEO capabilities baked in to increase search visibility, so you don’t have to do the heavy lifting with the technical stuff.

Expand your website content — if you want to boost your sales, providing more information for your customers is key. This might include details about your menu and your story, things people often want to know.
Additionally, the content of your website makes you unique and stand out from other restaurants on the block, which can encourage customers to come back and spend money with you.
Now, how do you stand out with content? There’s no shortage of ways, so let’s dive in.

Depending on your restaurant style, you may want to consider offering online ordering. Even if you only offer your online ordering for pickup, the convenience of quick takeout can be a selling point for your customers. Using Owner.com, you can also set up simple and affordable delivery, using a network of top-rated drivers in your area.

Ensure your website prominently features an online ordering button at the top for easy access. Owner.com enables you to create your own online delivery system, facilitating commission-free deliveries through your website and utilizing third-party driver networks.

Direct ordering from your site can be more cost-effective for customers than apps, fostering repeat business and increased spending. It's a game-changer, and it's as amazing as it sounds. Take a look at how Sauce the City used Owner.com to showcase its delivery page.
Pro Tip: To keep customers ordering through your website, offer a loyalty system — I’ll dive into this in the next point.

A restaurant website is important for driving direct orders, and a loyalty program is a simple yet effective strategy to offer perks and show gratitude for their patronage. Implementing a loyalty program is an excellent marketing tactic for restaurants because it:

items.title: Include Your Menu
items.body: The most important piece of content on your website will be your restaurant menu. If a customer comes across your menu and it’s cluttered and hard to read, they may not pick your restaurant for their Saturday night dinner plans, and you could lose a sale.

items.title: Tell Your Story On an About Page
items.body: Does a restaurant really need an “about us” page? After all, we already talked about why most people visit your site — for the menu and location, right? That’s true. And yet, you should absolutely include an “about us” page because it’s a great opportunity to tell your story.

items.title: Show Customers How to Book With You
items.body: Providing a space for your reservation details is an easy way to make sure customers know how to book with you and can generate business. While you can provide an online form that you manage yourself, an integration with reservation software, like OpenTable or Resy, may provide a better user experience.

items.title: List Contact Information and Social Media
items.body: Including your contact information is an obvious one — include your address, email, and phone number on your site. You should also include your social media accounts.

items.title: Use High-Quality Images to Attract Visitors
items.body: We’ve talked a lot about written content so far, but we haven’t talked about something equally important — images. Food is visual, right? We’ve all heard the saying, “People eat with their eyes.” Going out to eat is an experience that entices all the senses. Unfortunately, you can’t harness smell, taste, or touch over the internet.

items.title: Spotlight Customer Testimonials and Reviews
items.body: These days, no one goes anywhere without checking online first. As many as 94% of people will pick a restaurant based on its online reviews. You’ve earned those good reviews. So, make them work for you by including some of your best reviews on your website in a Reviews or Testimonials section.

items.title: Showcase Upcoming Events
items.body: There are several reasons to list all of your events on your site, even if you already do on social media. For starters, not everyone who visits your website will also check your Facebook or Instagram. They might be awfully disappointed to show up for dinner, just to find that you’re closed for a private event that night.

We’ve helped thousands of restaurants drive over $100 million in sales and learned what truly works. In this guide, I’ll walk you through a proven restaurant marketing strategy to:
💡 Think about restaurant marketing advertising in a way most overlook.
🗑️ Stop wasting money on restaurant marketing tactics that don’t pay off.
📈 Build a restaurant marketing strategy that drives results.
This is the same approach we’ve used to help restaurants grow for years, boosting their online orders by an average of 270% in just 90 days.
The 4 Ps of restaurant marketing are product, price, promotion, and place. Together, they form the foundation of any effective marketing strategy.

Social media marketing can cost as little or as much as you want. If you’re handling content yourself, your main investment is time. If you’re running paid ads, even a small budget (like a few dollars a day) can drive results if your targeting and content are solid. The key is to start small, see what works, and scale from there instead of overspending upfront.

Focus on the fundamentals that help nearby diners find you: put your cuisine and location keywords (like "best tacos in West Loop") in your homepage title and headline, publish your menu as real crawlable text rather than a PDF, and make sure your site loads fast on mobile. Then strengthen your local presence by claiming and optimizing your Google Business Profile and keeping your name, address, and phone number consistent everywhere online. For the full playbook, see our guides on restaurant SE

Make sure your name, address, and phone number are accurate and consistent across Google and all other online directories. Add high-quality photos, keep your hours up to date, respond to reviews, and use relevant keywords in your business description. These steps help Google understand your restaurant and show it to local diners.

For small restaurants, simple points-based or visit-based programs often work best. They’re easy to understand, cost-effective and encourage repeat visits without requiring complex management. Offering rewards on high-margin items or signature dishes ensures profitability while keeping customers engaged.

On average, you should aim to post on your main feed about five times per week, with two or three Stories daily. Again, this will vary from restaurant to restaurant. Check your engagement numbers to see if you’re posting too much or not enough.

That depends on the type of software. But in general, look for tools that help you save time, cut costs and boost sales. Key features to look for include online ordering, POS, inventory tracking, team scheduling, reservations and built-in marketing. The best software grows with your restaurant, not against it.

Start by securing a domain name, then choose how you'll build it — a website builder is the fastest, no-code route for most owners. From there, add the essential pages (menu, about, contact, and online ordering), optimize the site for local SEO so nearby diners can find you, and make sure it loads fast on mobile. Finally, connect your Google Business Profile and promote the site before going live.

content.heading: How to Create a Restaurant App (Without Being a Developer)
content.subheading: What is a branded restaurant app?
body: Fifty-seven percent of adults now use mobile ordering, including 74% of millennials and 65% of Gen Z. We'll show you how to build an app that increases sales and enhances customer loyalty.

As a restaurant owner, you don’t have time to babysit slow, clunky ordering systems. In a recent report, 57% of adults used mobile ordering. Adoption climbs even higher among younger customers, with 74% of millennials and 65% of Gen Z using it.
That means faster checkouts, fewer abandoned orders, and more money staying in your pocket instead of going to third-party marketplaces.

But speed isn’t the only reason to consider a restaurant app. The right app makes it easy for customers to reorder, rewards loyalty, and keeps your brand front and center every time they think about their next meal.
In this guide, I’ll show you exactly how to create a branded app for your restaurant, without being (or hiring!) a developer.

A branded restaurant app is a mobile app that carries your restaurant's own name, logo, and design, available for customers to download. On your app, guests can browse your menu, order online directly, earn loyalty rewards, and get push notifications from you. Unlike listing your restaurant on a third-party marketplace like DoorDash or Uber Eats, a branded app is yours: your brand on the customer's home screen, your relationship with the guest, and every order placed commission-free.

That home-screen presence is what makes it so powerful. A branded app turns first-time visitors into repeat regulars by making reordering effortless, and it gives you direct marketing channels to bring customers back without paying for ads each time. Because customers own the app and you own the data, it becomes one of your most valuable assets for driving repeat orders and long-term customer lifetime value.

Here's the part that trips most owners up: you might assume building an app means hiring an expensive developer or learning to code. That used to be true, but it isn't anymore. Modern restaurant app platforms like Owner build, launch, and maintain a fully branded app for you — no developers, no code, and no five-figure agency invoice — so you get all the benefits of a custom app without the traditional cost or complexity.

If you’re serious about growing your restaurant, a mobile app is no longer optional. Your guests already live on their phones, and if ordering from you isn’t seamless there, they’ll go somewhere else. Here are three practical reasons I believe every restaurant should have its own mobile app.
When I look at real ordering behavior, one trend jumps out. Diners clearly prefer mobile apps for digital orders.
I’ve seen the data behind thousands of restaurant mobile apps. For the right cuisine, they’re proven to increase reorder rates:
Restaurants with apps get 112% more return customers than restaurants without an app. What’s more, regulars who use a restaurant’s app order twice as much as non-app customers.
And when you factor in loyalty programs? Our internal data has found that regulars who join your app’s rewards program order 17% more often. Which can make apps hugely profitable.
Having your own app gets your regulars to order directly from your restaurant, cutting out the fees charged by third-party delivery platforms.

Guests still enjoy the convenience they expect, and highlighting the money they save when ordering from your app encourages them to order more frequently. Over time, these savings add up and have a noticeable impact on your bottom line.
A well-designed app makes ordering fast and easy. Customers can place orders in seconds, save their favorite meals, and check out instantly with payment options like Apple Pay.
Push notifications and pre-ordering options keep your restaurant top-of-mind and encourage repeat visits.

If you’re thinking about a mobile app for your restaurant, don’t overcomplicate it. I’ve seen owners stall for months because they think building an app means hiring a huge tech team or rebuilding their entire operation—it doesn’t. You just need a clear plan and the right partner.

‍Before you look at any tools, get clear on what you actually want the app to do. Is your goal to increase repeat orders? Push loyalty? Reduce third-party fees? Increase average check size? If you don't define the outcome, you'll end up paying for features you don't need. I always tell owners to start with the business problem first—the tech comes second. Write down your must-haves and nice-to-haves, and you'll pick the right solution much faster.

‍This is the step that's changed the most. You used to need a custom development agency and a five-figure budget; now the smarter move for almost every independent restaurant is a done-for-you platform built specifically for restaurants. Look for one that handles the build, the app-store submissions, and ongoing updates for you—so there's no code, no maintenance headaches, and no surprise invoices. Make sure it's restaurant-specific (not a generic app builder), with online ordering, loyalty, and

‍With the right platform, "design" isn't a coding project—it's a setup step. Your app should feel simple, fast, and on-brand: your logo and colors up front, clear menus with visible prices, easy customization, and frictionless checkout. The test I always use: can a guest place an order in under a minute without getting confused? A good platform gives you a proven layout that already clears that bar, so you just add your branding and menu.

‍Your app needs to work with your ordering, menu, loyalty, and ordering—and the whole point of an all-in-one platform is that these connect automatically instead of you patching tools together after launch. When everything runs on one system, orders flow straight to your kitchen, menus stay synced everywhere, and your reporting lives in one clean dashboard. No integrations to manage, no manual work, no preventable mistakes.

‍Launching the app is the starting line, not the finish. You need to actively push guests to download it—promote it in-store, on receipts, on social media, and through email and SMS marketing. Give people a reason to try it, whether that's bonus loyalty points or an app-only offer. The restaurants that win don't just build an app; they consistently remind guests to use it.

If you’re going to invest in a restaurant mobile app, it has to actually drive revenue. I’ve seen plenty of restaurant apps that look nice but don’t move the needle because they’re missing the basics. These six features consistently increase orders, repeat visits, and average ticket size.

items.title: The 6 must-have features of restaurant mobile apps
1. No-hassle sign-up experience
items.body: Getting a guest to download your app is a big deal—that screen real estate is precious. Keep sign-up simple: Only ask for essential info like phone and email. You can request payment details later at checkout, when guests are motivated to complete an order.

items.title: 2. Fast and easy online ordering
items.body: Ordering should be fast and frictionless. Floating “add to order” buttons with prices right on them make scrolling the menu actually tempting. Apple Pay and Google Pay? One-tap checkout is so much more convenient. And don’t block checkout just because delivery isn’t available—let guests choose takeout or schedule for later.

items.title: 3. Simple (but powerful) in-app rewards
items.body: Rewards programs increase engagement by showing clear progress toward goals. Start guests with a few points so they feel a head start, and show progress everywhere: banners on menu items and a rewards overview page. This motivates repeat orders and keeps guests coming back.

items.title: ‍4. Easy to browse menu
items.body: Your menu has to look as good on a phone as it does on the plate. Rich photos, clear descriptions, and a “popular items” section make browsing easier for everyone. Even regulars sometimes need a nudge, and a well-designed menu does that without you saying a word.

items.title: 5. Smart upsells built right into the app
items.body: High-margin items like sides, drinks, and desserts should be suggested at key moments: in the cart, at checkout, or after adding an item. Make it simple with one-tap additions and clearly show menu prices. Offer profitable customizations like premium ingredients or dietary modifications.

items.title: 6. Ability to showcase your unique brand
items.body: Your app should reflect your restaurant’s personality. Use strong visuals, a consistent voice, and copy that communicates your brand while keeping ordering simple. A single hero image, color palette, and smart copy can make even a no-frills app feel distinctive.

items.title: POS Integration
items.body: If your app doesn’t sync directly with your point of sale (POS), your team ends up re-entering orders by hand. That slows down the line, increases mistakes, and creates headaches during a rush. With proper POS sync, every app order appears instantly in your POS system, just like an in-store order. The kitchen receives the order automatically, the right prep station sees it immediately, and sales totals update in real time.

content.heading: Local SEO for Restaurants: 8 Tips To Get Your Restaurant Found by Local Customers
content.subheading: The easiest way to grow your restaurant online
body: I’ll show you how to master your local SEO, create an optimized Google Business Profile and ensure consistent online listings so your restaurant is the top choice in local searches.

When someone nearby pulls out their phone and searches "best tacos near me" or "pizza delivery in [your city]," one restaurant gets the click — and the order. Local SEO for restaurants is how you make sure that restaurant is yours. It's the practice of getting your restaurant to show up at the top of Google's map pack, on Google Maps, and in "near me" searches at the exact moment hungry customers in your area are deciding where to eat.

Here's the encouraging part: you're not competing against every one of the million-plus restaurants in the U.S. — just the handful in your neighborhood. That makes local search one of the highest-ROI ways to win new customers and drive direct, commission-free orders.
In this guide, we'll break down how local SEO actually works and walk through the proven steps to rank higher, get found by more diners, and turn local searches into real revenue.

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.

items.title: What is Local SEO for Restaurants?
items.body: Local SEO for restaurants is the practice of optimizing your restaurant's online presence so it shows up when nearby customers search for a place to eat — in Google's local "map pack," on Google Maps, and in "near me" and "best [food] in [city]" in Google search results.

items.title: What is the Difference Between SEO and Local SEO?
items.body: Restaurant SEO is the broad practice of getting your restaurant's website to rank in Google's standard search results for any relevant query — things like "gluten-free pasta" "best brunch spots," or "how much to tip catering." It's about your site's content, keywords, page speed, and links, and it isn't tied to a specific location. ‍Local SEO is a subset of SEO — the geographic slice that focuses on getting your restaurant found by nearby diners in the moments they're deciding where to eat. Inst

items.title: How Does Local SEO for Restaurants Work?
items.body: Google decides which restaurants to show for local searches based on three factors: 1. Relevance: how well your business matches the search 2. Distance: how close you are to the searcher 3. Prominence: how well-known and trusted you are, based on reviews, citations, and links. You influence these signals mainly through your Google Business Profile (accurate categories, hours, and photos) plus a steady flow of positive reviews, consistent name-address-phone info (NAP) across the web, and a fast,

items.title: How To Do Local SEO For Restaurants (8 Easy Tips)
items.body: Now that we understand what local SEO is, why it matters for restaurants, and how Google ranks restaurants in local search, you're probably asking yourself: "How do I actually do Local SEO for my restaurant?".

items.title: 1. Set up your Google Business Profile
items.body: If you haven’t already, set up your Google Business Profile. Your Google Business Profile (GBP) listing is the first thing that pops up when someone searches for your restaurant and shows important details like your business contact information, hours and directions. Plus, you can do it for free!

items.title: 2. Create a Restaurant Website
items.body: Your Google Business Profile gets you found; your restaurant website is what turns that discovery into a decision. Think of them as a one-two punch of local SEO for restaurants. The Google Business Profile wins the map pack and the "near me" search, and the website backs it up with the menu, story, and ordering experience that convince a hungry diner to actually choose you. Google sees the two as connected, too — a fast, credible website linked from your profile reinforces your legitimacy and he

items.title: 3. Optimize your restaurant website with keywords
items.body: Using keywords on your website that reflect your business tells Google that your restaurant is relevant. The key is to understand what terms people are searching for when they want to spend their money at a restaurant like yours.

items.title: 4. Create a great online menu
items.body: Your online menu is one of the most-visited and most-searched parts of your entire online presence. Potential diners routinely look it up before they ever decide to order or walk in. It's also prime SEO real estate, because every dish name is a keyword. Someone searching "birria tacos near me" or "gluten-free pizza in [city]" can only find you if those items actually live in text on your site, which makes your menu a direct line to high-intent, ready-to-order searchers.

items.title: 5. Encourage reviews from customers
items.body: Google loves restaurants with lots of reviews because it shows that people are talking about and engaging with your place. Reviews are also like digital word of mouth — customers are more likely to check out a restaurant if previous customers liked it.

items.title: 6. Ensure your restaurant listings are accurate
items.body: Your Google Business Profile might be the most important listing, but it isn't the only one you should care about. Not only should you make sure that you have profiles set up on the most common and popular listing site, you should also make sure that your restaurant name, address and phone number (NAP) are all the same everywhere that it’s posted. When Google sees this consistency, it knows your info is solid and reliable and will show your restaurant to more potential customers. Double-check si

items.title: 7. Join forces with local outlets
items.body: Want more people to find you? Reach out to local newspapers, food blogs and guides to see if they’ll feature your restaurant.

items.title: 8. Boost your social media efforts
items.body: Social media may not directly help your local SEO like setting up your GBP will, but it can get others to talk about your restaurant, attract the local community and drive more sales. Social media isn’t usually the most time-efficient for restaurants, which is why it ranks lower on the list. But once you've got a handle on these local SEO tips, it starts to make a lot more sense to put some effort into it.

items.title: Bonus Tip: Optimize for AI Search
items.body: Google's AI Overviews and tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity are fast becoming where customers discover restaurants, and they pull from the same foundations as your Maps rankings: your Google Business Profile, your website content, your reviews, and consistent citations across the web. The restaurants that surface in AI recommendations are the ones with accurate, complete business information and strong reputation signals — so good local SEO is already most of the battle.

items.title: How should restaurants measure local SEO?
items.body: The point of local SEO isn't rankings for their own sake — it's more diners finding you and ordering. So measure it from two angles: the visibility signals that show you're climbing, and the business outcomes that prove it's working.

items.title: Upgrade your website to increase local visibility
items.body: Getting noticed by new customers in your neighborhood is all about having a killer website. When your site looks sharp and has all the details mentioned in this post, it tells Google that your restaurant is a hot spot and worth showing off. Plus, having a top-notch website beefs up your GBP listing, which is crucial for local SEO success.

body: I’ll compare the top website builders for restaurants by function, cost and more to determine which will best support your business goals.

Choosing a restaurant website builder can be frustrating. There are endless options, and after hours of research (scanning lists, reading Reddit threads, etc.), you still might not have a clear answer.
Here’s why: There’s no single “best” restaurant website builder.
The real question isn’t which builder is the best—it’s which website builder is best for your restaurant. They all create websites, but the right choice depends on your goals.

For example, if you want to increase direct online orders without spending hours tweaking a website, you’ll need a builder that prioritizes seamless ordering and automation. But if your focus is on driving more dine-in reservations and showcasing your cuisine, a highly customizable site with rich visuals might be a better fit.
Two goals, two very different website builders. This guide will help you find the best match for your needs.
Budget also plays a major factor in this decision. Cheapest isn't always best, but restaurant owners also need to keep budget in mind.

Full disclosure: We included Owner.com in this list, but we’re not the best fit for everyone. But by the end, you’ll have all the information you need to help you choose a platform that works best for your restaurant.
Our recommendations in this article are based on two things: our own research and what we hear from restaurant owners every day.

Research: we spent days manually testing every single restaurant website builder option on this list. We approached it through the lens of a website owner who needs to drive visibility and sales, but maybe isn't the most technical person on the planet. What we hear from restaurant owners: we talk to hundreds of restaurant owners every single day. When restaurant owners switch to our platform, they tell us what they don’t like about the website builder they are leaving. And when restaurants leave
Getting this constant feedback from restaurant owners is super helpful. It gives us a clear, updated understanding of what restaurant owners must consider when choosing their website builder.
My goal with this post is to help you pick the website builder for your restaurant, even if it’s not us.
When restaurant owners compare website builders, they usually ask these questions:
Design customization is important for owners of upscale restaurants. Or for those concepts where the vibes are a big part of the dining experience. Think: lounges, omakase, steakhouses, etc.

For those kinds of restaurants, perception is important. That means a unique website design is important. It has to feel like your own restaurant website, not anyone else's. Which means you need a website builder that is strong on customization.
So if a unique design is your top priority, here’s how popular website builders compare:

Wix and WordPress are the best options if you care a lot about design flexibility. Both platforms have almost unlimited possibilities, but that comes with a cost – both time and hiring someone to customize your site for you. Bentobox, Popmenu and Squarespace offer some design flexiblity, while Owner.com and Square Online are very limited in their freedom of design, but for good reason. ‍ I’ll soon go into detail and explain why each builder is ranked this way.
But for now, let’s look at the second question:
Some restaurant owners see their website as having one main job: drive online orders.

They want their online presence to increase direct sales. These owners usually have a goal to save how much they pay to third party delivery apps. I see this often in takeout-heavy cuisines: pizza, sushi, Thai, tacos, etc.

For these restaurant owners, the top priority isn’t design – it’s to get more sales online. This means choosing a website builder that is strong on features for search engine optimization and driving direct orders. Sure, design is important, but not the main thing.
If your goal is increasing direct online orders, here’s how the restaurant website builders rank:

Owner.com is the strongest option for restaurant owners who care about driving more online orders. With online ordering built into every Owner.com website, our customers consistently see huge online ordering growth within just a few weeks. Bentobox, Square Online and Popmenu also offer online ordering capabilities, while adding online ordering to Squarespace, WordPress and Wix is not so straightforward or effective. content.heading: 93% of Restaurant Guests Will Download Your Mobile App (But Only if It Has These Key Benefits)
content.subheading: The easiest way to grow your restaurant online
body: What drives guests to use your restaurant’s mobile app? We surveyed them to find out—here are the 6 most important takeaways.
What convinces guests to use your restaurant’s mobile app?

I’ve spoken with many restaurant owners about this exact question. Some had guesses, but very few had hard data to back them up. That’s because, until now, data on how guests interact with mobile apps was limited.

We surveyed over 1,300 guests in the US to understand how they use restaurant mobile apps. What features do they care about most? What makes them download an app, and just as important, what keeps them using it?
Owner’s survey data sheds light on these questions—and today, I’m excited to share the top 6 takeaways.

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.

items.title: Takeaway #1: 93% of guests are willing to download mobile apps from their favorite restaurants
items.body: “Will guests really download an app?” Our case studies have confidently told us, “Yes, absolutely.” But there’s still skepticism from some restaurant owners who think apps are only for Gen Z.

items.title: Takeaway #2: Guests are much more likely to use mobile apps if they’re a “regular,” which starts with as little as 2 orders per month
items.body: So, who will be the primary customer on your restaurant’s mobile app? “Regulars,” or those who order from you relatively frequently.

items.title: Takeaway #3: 83% of guests find mobile apps more convenient and make them more likely to reorder from a restaurant
items.body: Regulars and frequent guests find mobile apps more convenient to reorder from than your website. Even the best restaurant websites that focus on ease-of-use and convenience will find it hard to compete with the two- or three-tap reordering process in well-made mobile apps.

items.title: Takeaway #4: Reward programs and exclusive deals are the main reasons guests stick with your restaurant’s mobile app
items.body: We know guests are drawn to mobile apps for the convenience—specifically, fast checkout and easy reordering. Beyond that, the features most likely to get guests to keep using your mobile app are exclusive discounts for trying (and retrying) the app, and the built-in rewards program.

items.title: Takeaway #5: 85% of guests look for a loyalty program in your app and the same number will take advantage of the rewards
items.body: Guests’ favorite feature in your app is a built-in restaurant loyalty program. You do have one of those, right? Trained by mega-brands like Starbucks and Domino’s, the vast majority of guests expect a rewards program and plan to take advantage of the rewards you offer.

items.title: Takeaway #6: Guests value photos of menu items just as much as on your website—and look for ways to save their favorites
items.body: Think menu photos don’t matter on mobile? Think again. 85% of guests said they frequently look for photos of menu items in your mobile app. I was shocked to learn that guests look for photos on mobile apps even more often than they do on your website—as shown by our previous survey.

18 Proven Restaurant Promotion Ideas That Work in 2026
content.subheading: The easiest way to grow your restaurant online
body: This is your complete guide to restaurant promotion, packed full of proven ideas that have helped real local restaurants grow their business.

Restaurant promotions aren't just about getting people through the door (though that's a big part of it) — they're also about building buzz, fostering loyalty, and keeping those cash registers ringing. If you’re looking for ways to make this happen and grow your restaurant — you’re in luck. This guide is packed full of proven ideas that have worked for real, local restaurants just like yours.

I’ve worked closely with thousands of restaurant owners over the last few years, and these are the exact promotion strategies they’ve used to grow consistently — month in and month out — with many achieving their goal of expanding to multiple new locations.
Read more to learn 18 ways you can take advantage of restaurant promotion and attract customers to drive sales.

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.

items.title: ‍1. Offer Loyalty Rewards
items.body: Connect with your customers (and get them to spend more money with you) and add a loyalty program — it’s a quick and easy way to offer promotions and discounts and give appreciation for their business.

items.title: 2. Partner With Third-Party Apps
items.body: You can add a lot of revenue to your bottom line by partnering with third-party apps to help with your restaurant promotion, like DoorDash. These apps have millions of users — that’s a lot of eyeballs (and hungry stomachs) you can tap into. Some smart ways to partner with an app like DoorDash, Uber Eats, or GrubHub and attract new customers include:

items.title: 3. Give a Personalized Discount Based on Order History
items.body: Promoting to your existing customers is just as important as promoting to get new customers, if not more. This is because getting a new customer can cost up to five times more than keeping an existing one. So, do you want to know a cool trick to keep your current customers coming back for more? Personalized discounts based on their past orders.

items.title: 4. Make Your Customers Famous on Instagram
items.body: People love a bit of digital validation, so why not give it to them on your restaurant’s Instagram by making them famous for a day? Encourage your customers to post pictures of your delicious-looking meals and pick a winner once a week/month for a free meal. Having your customers do this simple act keeps them engaged and happy with their freebie, and you get easy restaurant promotion in return.

items.title: 5. Let Your Customers Peek Behind the Curtain
items.body: You may see your restaurant as just a normal business, but to a diner, there is always a little bit of intrigue about what happens behind the scenes. If you have a new dish, that’s your new baby to show the world.

items.title: 6. Pop-Up Somewhere Unexpected
items.body: We’re willing to bet your community has a reasonably busy calendar of events throughout the year, especially in the warmer months. Places to set up a small pop-up restaurant could be places like:

items.title: 7. Get on Top of Your Google My Business Listing
items.body: Picture this — a potential customer is feeling hunger pangs, and they Google your restaurant name, but they can’t see your opening hours right away. Just like that, you’ve lost them. That may sound over the top, but people expect this information immediately, or they’ll simply lose patience and move on.

items.title: 8. Answer That Bad Review
items.body: Look, we get it. Reading people’s complaints about your restaurant isn’t high up on your daily to-do list. But even if it’s a trivial complaint, responding to their criticism in a meaningful and friendly way is a powerful restaurant promotion tool for your reputation. This is something that should be high priority, as 53% of customers expect businesses to follow up on a bad review within one week.

items.title: 9. Provide a Percentage Discount
items.body: This is as simple as it gets, but percentage discount promotions are consistently the most profitable campaigns for our restaurant partners here at Owner.com. These types of campaigns work for every restaurant and customer type. The key is to run ads with strong copywriting that grabs attention and asks the user a question the customer will answer “yes” to in their head:

items.title: 10. Host a Customer Challenge or Contest
items.body: People love to be challenged. “I bet you $30 you can’t finish 3 pounds of burger in one sitting.” This is how you get people to show up to your restaurant and order $30 mega-burgers.

items.title: ‍11. Take Advantage of the Holidays
items.body: Holidays can be a massive source of new business, but they also bring their fair share of competition. Every restaurant in your area is going to be running promotions and specials to compete for that holiday dining dash. You could try restaurant marketing ideas like:

items.title: 12. Support a Charity
items.body: We’re sure you have a cause close to your heart, so why not let your customers know and invite them to participate? Designating a weekly night where a percentage of profits goes to a specific charity allows you to:

items.title: 13. Go Viral
items.body: Getting your restaurant to go viral can be a game-changer for your business, but it often requires a combination of creativity, strategic restaurant marketing, and providing an exceptional customer experience.

items.title: 14. Offer a BOGO Deal
items.body: While BOGO (buy one, get one free) offers tend to be associated more with fast and casual restaurants, they can be used effectively by virtually any restaurant.

items.title: 15. Mix Things Up With a Secret Menu
items.body: How about creating a secret menu item? You know, something special that only the insiders know about. This could be a unique dish that's only available upon request for those in the know. It creates a sense of exclusivity and excitement, encouraging customers to come back to discover what's new and hidden.

items.title: 16. Create a Limited-Run Menu Item
items.body: Promotions are all about getting customers to take action, and few things motivate action quite like a deadline. Limited-run menu items are an ideal promotion strategy for several reasons:

Your restaurant's point of sale (POS) system controls every transaction, order, and guest interaction in your restaurant. Quick-service restaurants need POS systems that prioritize speed and efficiency. Look for fast order processing, mobile ordering integration, kitchen display systems for accurate order routing, and simple menu customization that lets you update items quickly during peak hours.
Employee management tools and basic inventory tracking are also valuable for managing high-volume operations without slowing down service.

Multi-location chains benefit most from cloud-based POS systems that offer centralized management and reporting. Systems like Toast, Aloha Cloud, and Lightspeed provide the ability to manage menus, pricing, and inventory across multiple locations from a single dashboard.

content.heading: 11 Best Restaurant Loyalty Programs That Drive Sales
body: I’ll show you how top brands maximize the profitability of their loyalty programs and how you can do it, too.

I’ll admit a nerdy secret: I love analyzing the loyalty programs that top restaurant brands build. National chains invest heavily in rewards, making them a useful reference for how programs are designed and used across the industry.
That focus makes sense. Loyalty members tend to visit restaurants they’re enrolled with at about twice the rate of non-members, even though they spread visits across many brands.
In this post, I’ll highlight top restaurant loyalty program examples and what they do well, so you can model after them for your own program.
Running a loyalty program raises a lot of practical questions for restaurant owners. Below, I’ll answer a few questions you might have before you launch your own program.

For small restaurants, simple points-based or visit-based programs often work best. They’re easy to understand, cost-effective and encourage repeat visits without requiring complex management. Offering rewards on high-margin items or signature dishes ensures profitability while keeping customers engaged.

Start by estimating the average incremental revenue generated by a reward (extra visits or order size) versus the cost of the reward. Factor in margins on the rewarded items and the number of rewards likely redeemed.
The break-even point is reached when the revenue from repeat visits offsets the cost of the rewards—tracking this over time helps optimize your program.

Most modern POS systems, or platforms like Owner, offer direct loyalty program integration. This allows points tracking, reward redemption and customer data to flow seamlessly without manual updates. Integration ensures accurate accounting, makes rewards easy for staff to manage and provides actionable insights on customer behavior.

content.heading: The Top 6 Changes Impacting the Restaurant Industry in 2026
content.subheading: The easiest way to grow your restaurant online
body: We surveyed guests to uncover the biggest restaurant trends to watch for in the new year.

The restaurant business is changing a lot. As we look to 2026, there are some important food trends and customer shifts that restaurant owners need to know about. Understanding these changes can help you plan and stay flexible so your business is successful.

We asked 1,000 customers about their eating habits and restaurant trends. We found out they care more about prices than ever, like ordering online, and feel okay using apps to order from their favorite places.
Let’s see what those 1,000 customers said. But first, I’ll talk about what’s happening in the restaurant business right now. Let’s jump in!👇

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.

items.title: The current state of the restaurant industry
items.body: Running a restaurant is no easy job, and the past few years have made it even harder with inflation. Luckily, only 17% of restaurants fail within the first year, but there are still some challenges that owners are facing.

items.title: Trend #1: 77% of guests are ordering from restaurants as often or more frequently in the past year
items.body: The good news is that customers continue ordering food from restaurants despite economic concerns. Thirty-six percent of guests order more often than before, and 41% are ordering about the same. 32% said they’re trying out more new restaurants than usual in the past 12 months. And 40% of guests have ordered from a restaurant in the past month.

items.title: Trend #2: 63% of guests say convenience is crucial in their ordering decisions
items.body: Convenience of delivery or takeout is no longer a nice-to-have—it's a top priority for your guests. In fact, it’s very important for 63% of customers. That’s why it’s important to prioritize a smooth and easy ordering process.

items.title: Trend #3: Pricing is a top factor in trying new restaurants
items.body: Menu selection is a top reason that influences customers to try a new restaurant. People are looking at menus and asking themselves, “Is this worth it?” That’s why a solid, competitive menu pricing strategy is so important to attract new customers. 41% of guests said pricing is one of the key factors when trying a new restaurant.

items.title: Trend #4: Almost half of guests believe third-party delivery fees are unfair
items.body: Third-party delivery fees aren’t cheap. In fact, 49% of guests think that third-party delivery fees are too high.

items.title: Takeaway #5: 45% of guests are likely to abandon orders due to high fees
items.body: Abandoned carts mean money left on the table. Studies suggest that over 70% of carts are abandoned. Our survey found that 45% of guests are likely to abandon their orders because of high fees.

items.title: Takeaway #6: 39% of guests feel restaurant value has decreased over the past year
items.body: It’s no secret that guests are becoming more critical of the value they receive when dining out. Nearly 39% of people believe the value restaurants offer has gone downhill in the past year.

content.heading: 10 Creative Restaurant Menu Examples to Inspire Your Design
body: Check out 10 real restaurant menus, what makes each one work and how to apply the same tactics to your own.

Your menu is your best salesperson. It's working to turn that simple click into an order every time a customer lands on your page. The problem is that most restaurants treat it like an afterthought: a PDF uploaded to their website and forgotten. The restaurant menu examples in this post prove there's a better way.

I've pulled together 10 real restaurant menu design examples from Owner.com customer restaurant websites that are getting this right. For each one, I'll show you exactly what they do well and the specific tactics you can take and apply to your own menu today.
Whether you're building from scratch or refreshing what you have, you'll walk away knowing what a high-converting digital menu actually looks like and the psychology behind why it works.
For the ideal font size for a restaurant menu, I recommend a minimum of 10pt for body text—but if your customer base skews older, bump that to 12pt or larger.

You should absolutely include high-resolution images of your food. For casual dining, fast casual and cuisines that are unfamiliar to your customer base—think Ethiopian, Filipino or regional Indian—photos do real work. They remove the guesswork and make customers more confident when ordering something new.
I’d recommend doing a moderate to full menu design refresh every 12-18 months as a good rule of thumb.

Food trends shift, ingredient costs change and pricing that made sense 18 months ago may no longer reflect your margins. A refresh also gives you a natural opportunity to cut underperforming items, spotlight new ones

items.title: 1. Metro Pizza
items.body: What I love about Metro Pizza's restaurant menu design is how it anticipates customer behavior before customers even think about it. Fries and garlic bread appear in the appetizers section without any scrolling—and that's not an accident.

items.title: 2. Pita Yeero
items.body: Most restaurants treat catering as an afterthought. Pita Yeero built their entire menu around it—and it shows. Their "Catering Packages" section does something I love: it bundles the decision for the customer. "Greek Feast for 10 People, $174.99" is a far easier sell than asking someone to do the math themselves.

items.title: 3. Asian Mint
items.body: I love how Asian Mint's menu is deliberately built around its customers. For example, see "Mahjong Specials"—an $85 shareable platter designed for a specific occasion, marketed directly to a community they know walks through their doors.

items.title: 4. Henry Higgins Boiled Bagels
items.body: I notice immediately that Henry Higgins has structured their menu well around upsells. A single bagel is $2.25—but a dozen is $25. "Cream Cheese By the Pound" turns a condiment into its own revenue line, with six SKUs ranging from plain to house-smoked salmon.

items.title: 5. Crazy Good Kitchen
items.body: The first thing I see when I land on CGK's menu is a location selector. And that's exactly right for a multi-location brand. Instead of guessing which address to show, they put the customer in control from the start.

items.title: 6. Jerk N Go
items.body: Jerk N Go's all-black menu design is an immediate brand statement—it matches the bold, unapologetic food and sets them apart from every generic white-background menu.

items.title: 7. Saffron Indian Kitchen
items.body: What I find impressive about Saffron is how they use their menu to keep things fresh—literally. "April Appetizer Specials" and "April Entrée Specials" appear at the top of the menu, right below Popular.

items.title: 8. Deliche
items.body: Deliché opens with something most restaurant menus skip entirely—active promo codes front and center. Before a customer even browses, they already have a reason to order.

items.title: 9. Berry Forkin' Good
items.body: Berry Forkin' Good's menu is a masterclass in brand consistency. Splitting crepes into "Sweet" and "Savory" is a small structural choice that removes friction for customers who already know what they're in the mood for.

items.title: 10. Desta Ethiopian Kitchen
items.body: What I appreciate about Desta is how confidently they introduce unfamiliar dishes to new customers.

content.heading: The Real Restaurant Failure Rate Is Lower Than You Think (2026 Data)
body: You might have heard that 90% of restaurants fail in their first year. That's false! Here's the real failure rate for restaurants—and what causes them to fail.
You've probably heard the crazy restaurant trend that 90% of restaurants fail within the first five years of operations. Well, it’s not true.
Apparently, this number was originally shared on a TV advertisement with no source listed—and the myth grew from there. And to be honest, that bothers me!

As CEO of Owner.com, I get to personally meet hundreds of successful restaurant owners. They’ll be the first to tell you that this is a tough business. But it’s a very rewarding one, too. And if we go around telling people 90% of restaurants fail, we’ll see far fewer new restaurants started.
So let’s set the record straight! Time for us to play “Math vs. Myth” and get the actual data:

Hengam Stanfield is the co-founder of Mattenga's Pizzeria, a seven-location restaurant group in San Antonio, TX. A former electrical engineer turned restaurateur, she applies a data-driven mindset to operations and marketing. Her work has been featured in PMQ Pizza Magazine, INC., Food & Wine, and Martha Stewart Living. Mattenga's has been voted Best Pizza in San Antonio and named Pizzeria of the Year by Pizza Today.

items.title: What’s the real restaurant failure rate?
items.body: Only 17% of restaurants fail in their first year. And around 51% of restaurants survive past their 5th year in business.

items.title: So, why do restaurants end up failing?
items.body: The other week, I was at a major restaurant trade show.

items.title: 5 non-obvious reasons why restaurants fail
items.body: Luckily, if you know these ahead of time, I’ve seen that you can plan around them. And, in many cases, avoid these issues altogether.

items.title: Reason #1 – They fail to find menu-market fit
items.body: Menu-market fit means how well your menu fits the demands of your local market. Both parts of this equation matter.

items.title: Reason #2 – They fail to build a clear and distinct brand
items.body: Brand is the set of expectations people have when they think about your restaurant. When someone walks in your door, places an order, or tells a friend, “brand” is whatever they think of first.

items.title: Reason #3 – They don’t control their margins
items.body: The business that can spend the most to acquire each customer usually wins in the long run. That’s why margins matter—you have to make money on dishes even after service and marketing expenses.

items.title: Reason #4 – They fail to get repeat customers
items.body: Data shows regulars can make up to 65-80% of a typical restaurant’s profits. Unless you’re in a tourist area, regulars really matter.

items.title: Reason #5 – They ruin first impressions with a bad online experience
items.body: Can a bad website and online ordering really sink your restaurant?

content.heading: The easiest way to grow your restaurant online
28 Proven Restaurant Marketing Ideas to Drive More Sales
body: From leveraging SEO to optimizing your menu, I can show you proven ideas that can help you turn each customer interaction into a revenue-driving opportunity.

Restaurant marketing can feel like an overwhelming uphill battle. Every new article claims to have the magic bullet—throwing out a long list of ideas that barely scratch the surface. But here's the truth: Effective marketing isn't about trying every tactic under the sun. It's about knowing what actually works.
We've done the research, tested the strategies and compiled the best ideas—backed by data.
Want to drive new orders, design your menu around customer demand, or increase repeat business? We’re breaking down the marketing moves that will make a real impact on your bottom line.
Because, in this game, it's not just about getting people through the door—it's about making sure every customer is profitable from the first bite to the last.

Before starting your restaurant marketing, ensure your offerings match local tastes and reflect emerging food trends. Understanding this is key to thriving—and not understanding it is one of the top reasons why restaurants fail.
Below, I’ll break down how to figure out your menu market fit:
I’ve already covered these steps in our post about restaurant failure, but to recap, you’ll want to find gaps in what your customers are searching for and what your competitors aren’t offering.

You’ll want to use the Google Keyword Planner to find what people are searching for and what competitors are selling. After that, you’ll want to look into competitors' reviews to uncover what they’re missing and analyze those reviews using the 4Ps:
After you compile that information, you can define your ideal customer and shape your brand to match, which I’ll get into next.
Next, you’ll want to find your ideal customer. I like to start by splitting customers' characteristics into two categories: demographics and behaviors:
So for demographics, you’d take notes of factors like:
And for behaviors, you could ask:
Once you have an idea of your customer base, you’ll have a better idea of how to tailor your menu, what marketing messages to send and which promotion ideas could work for your customers.

Knowing who you're trying to feed is half the battle. Once you've nailed down your ideal customer, building your brand is like putting together a really fun puzzle. It's way better than staring at a blank canvas, right?
Your brand is a mix of what you sell, what you say and how you treat your customers. When these pieces fit together perfectly, you've got a winning formula.

Take Metro Pizza, for example. They nailed it by becoming the go-to pizza place for families in the suburbs. Their brand screams cozy, authentic and convenient: Metro Pizza | America’s Neighborhood Pizzeria Since 1928.
The key to growing your customer base is to make it as easy as possible for new customers to find and choose your restaurant.

From optimizing your online presence with Google search engine optimization (SEO) to creating eye-catching menu pages, every little detail counts. Think of it as setting the stage for potential customers who are already searching for exactly what you offer.
Now, I get it—SEO can sound complicated, but it doesn’t have to be. You don’t need to be a developer or spend hours tweaking your website.
In fact, a few simple changes can make a huge difference. That’s where the 80/20 rule comes in: 20% of the tweaks you make will drive 80% of the results.

Automating your marketing and SEO can also help you easily execute your restaurant marketing efforts without getting overwhelmed. So with that, here are my top promotional ideas that will help you gain more new customers:

Google SEO is one of the most effective ways to reach new customers, especially local diners. Unlike social media, which focuses more on discovery, Google connects you with people actively searching for a place to eat.

In fact, our latest data about restaurant trends shows that 77% of guests are ordering from restaurants as often or more frequently than in the past year. This makes it essential to show up when they're searching.

For example, Mo and Omar at Talkin’ Tacos found that Google SEO brought in seven times more customers than social media. Why? Because Google targets people in your area who are ready to make a purchase.

items.title: Manage your restaurant’s brand and reputation
22. Respond to and request reviews
items.body: One of the most important ways to manage your restaurant’s public image is by leveraging your customers' reviews. First off, you should always respond to customers’ reviews and address concerns or thank them for a kind message.

items.title: 23. Highlight seasonal promotions
items.body: Seasonal events are a great way to attract customers with targeted emails and promotions.

items.title: 24. Keep your listing updated
items.body: Keep your information up to date always. Nothing will spark a bad review quicker than if a customer shows up to a closed restaurant that was marked as open online.

items.title: 25. Collaborate with food bloggers and influencers
items.body: Collaborating with food bloggers and influencers can do wonders for our restaurant's brand and reputation. First, I suggest you find influencers and bloggers whose style and audience vibe with our brand, especially those with a strong local presence.

items.title: 26. Sponsor local events
items.body: Supporting your community by sponsoring local events, festivals or sports teams is a fantastic way to boost your restaurant's visibility and reach a broader audience. By getting involved, you not only show that you care about local happenings but also increase your brand's exposure.

items.title: 27. Create recurring promotions
items.body: Create recurring promotions to engage customers, like weekly or monthly specials featuring your flagship menu items.

items.title: 28. Try pop-up locations
items.body: Creating buzz can be as simple as popping up in unexpected places. Consider setting up a temporary location or hosting a special event in a unique spot to generate excitement. You could do something like offering a limited-time menu or hosting an exclusive event that draws attention and gets people talking about your restaurant.

items.title: Take your restaurant to the next level with these marketing ideas
items.body: Restaurant marketing is part coming up with ideas, and part experimenting. The right way to approach this list is to lean into your biggest marketing problem or opportunity, test a few ideas, and measure results.
